content: Teams of experts were tasked with evaluating the evidence for the PICO questions and their outcomes through systematic literature reviews, adhering to a standardized methodology. Titles, abstracts, and full texts of potentially relevant studies were screened using specific subject keywords and text words. Authors and field experts were contacted to identify any missing studies or ongoing research. Individual patient-level data were utilized to address PICO 1 (adults and children), PICO 3 (shorter MDR-TB regimens), and PICO 4 (use of surgery). Relative effects, such as relative risks or odds ratios, were calculated from pooled data in individual or aggregated formats from the included studies. Absolute effects and risk differences were used to quantify the magnitude of an effect or the difference between intervention and comparator groups. Adjustments were made, where possible, to minimize bias and confounding. The certainty of the evidence was assessed using criteria such as study design, limitations in the studies (risk of bias), imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness, publication bias, magnitude of effect, dose-response relationships, and residual confounding. More details on the GRADE evidence profiles, which summarize the results of systematic reviews for each question, are provided in the accompanying notes. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) included a diverse representation of future guideline users and affected individuals, including patients. Before the GDG meeting held at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, from November 9 to 11, 2015, discussants from the GDG were identified to evaluate the evidence for each PICO question and present their perspectives on the findings during the meeting. Additional analyses were shared with the group during and after the meeting as requested. The GRADE evidence profiles were reviewed by the GDG before formulating recommendations. The group used Evidence to Decision tables via the GRADEPro interface to document discussions, make judgments, annotate considerations, develop the wording and strength of recommendations, and add remarks accompanying each recommendation. The strength of a recommendation was determined by assessing the balance between desirable and undesirable effects, values and preferences, equity, resource use, and feasibility. The GDG paid particular attention to the spectrum of values and preferences associated with the recommendations by different users. Variability in these values and preferences was a significant factor that weakened the strength of all recommendations in these guidelines. Resource use was assessed from the perspectives of patients and health services in terms of feasibility and opportunity cost, rather than through formal cost-effectiveness studies. Decisions on the certainty of evidence, the wording of recommendations, and their strength were made through moderated discussions. Disagreements were resolved by group consensus. For the recommendation on surgery (part of PICO 4), the final wording was agreed upon through voting. None of the recommendations in these guidelines were strong, and the certainty of the evidence was rated as very low. The External Review Group (ERG) provided feedback on the questions during their formulation in mid-2015 and on a draft of the guidelines, including the recommendations, following comments from the GDG in February 2016. Six reviewers provided substantial comments on the draft guidelines. The guidelines and evidence reviews are available as freely downloadable PDF files and will also be published in peer-reviewed journals to enhance dissemination. The 2017 update of the drug-susceptible TB treatment guidelines aimed to revise the evidence-based policy recommendations from the 2010 guidelines. This update included additional evidence-based recommendations on cross-cutting issues relevant to patient care and support for patients with drug-susceptible or drug-resistant TB. The decentralized model of care for drug-resistant TB patients, previously unaddressed by WHO TB guidelines, was also included for evidence assessment. The WHO Guidelines Steering Group and GDG prioritized questions for the update by focusing on areas of drug-susceptible TB treatment and care that had not been addressed by previous guidelines and for which evidence was expected to be available. They also considered areas where new evidence had emerged that could lead to changes in existing recommendations. The scope of the guidelines was limited to priority areas, such as treatment interruption or recurrence of disease and the effectiveness of decentralized care models for MDR-TB. The guidelines include GRADE-assessed recommendations and aim to address the needs of a wide variety of health workers and audiences. Separate how-to guidance will be developed later to provide additional information on implementing the recommendations. WHO's Global TB Programme aims to consolidate essential guidance on managing drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB into a single guideline. The recommendations in these guidelines qualify both their strength and the certainty of the evidence on which they are based. Certainty in the evidence is categorized into four levels: high, moderate, low, and very low. High certainty indicates that further research is unlikely to change confidence in the effect estimate, while very low certainty means the effect estimate is highly uncertain. The text of each recommendation should be read alongside accompanying remarks summarizing the evidence, anticipated effects, and other considerations important for policy implementation.
